target: Ellos están sentados en la terraza.
english: They're sitting on the terrace.
tip: English sees an action (they are sitting); Spanish sees a state: están sentados = they are seated. Están sentándose would mean they're in the very act of lowering themselves into chairs.

target: La reunión es a las diez.
english: The meeting is at ten.
tip: Ser for scheduled events: La reunión es a las diez.

english: Is there a map of the city?
tip: Hay un mapa asks whether one exists at all; ¿Está el mapa? would ask about one specific, known map. Existence pairs hay with un – a known thing takes estar with el.

target: El problema es que no hay sitio.
english: The problem is that there's no room.
tip: El problema – ends in -a but is masculine (Greek origin: -ema, -ama).

english: We write to each other on WhatsApp.
tip: "Escribirse" = to write to each other. The "se" here is reciprocal: "Nos escribimos" = We write to each other.

english: How much does this T-shirt cost?
tip: Cuesta agrees with the T-shirt, not with you – the item is the subject doing the costing. Shopping for two things? ¿Cuánto cuestan? The question pluralizes along with the goods.

english: I'm fed up with excuses.
tip: 'Estar harto de' = to be fed up with. 'Estar' is used for emotional/temporary states, not 'ser'.

english: On Sundays we eat as a family.
tip: Los domingos = on Sundays (definite article + day = habitual).

target: Esta carta es para el director.
english: This letter is for the director.
tip: "Para" = for (recipient): "Este regalo es para ti." Para marks who receives something.

target: Estamos listos para empezar la presentación.
english: We're ready to start the presentation.
tip: Estar + listo = ready (temporary). Ser + listo = clever (inherent trait).

target: Me fijo mucho en los detalles.
english: I pay close attention to details.
tip: "Fijarse en" = to notice / pay attention to. Always reflexive + en: "¿Te fijaste en eso?" = Did you notice that?

target: ¿A qué hora se acuestan los niños?
english: What time do the kids go to bed?
tip: Acostar means to put someone to bed; the se bends it back onto the kids – they put themselves to bed. Drop the se and you'd be asking what time they tuck someone else in.

target: Mi tío es médico en un hospital.
english: My uncle is a doctor in a hospital.
tip: Spanish drops 'a' before jobs: es médico, never es un médico. The article only returns when you add an adjective – es un médico excelente.

target: Las cortinas del dormitorio no dejan pasar la luz.
english: The bedroom curtains don't let the light through.
tip: Dejar + infinitive = let something happen: no dejan pasar la luz. Note the order – la luz comes after pasar, the reverse of English 'let the light through.'

target: ¿A cuánto estamos hoy? Estamos a veintiséis de marzo.
english: What's the date today? It's the twenty-sixth of March.
tip: For dates Spanish asks where you 'are' on the calendar: ¿A cuánto estamos? Estamos a veintiséis – literally 'we're at the 26th' of the month.

english: Did you get my email?
tip: ¿Recibiste? – one email, one moment of arrival, done. If you can pin an action to a single point in time, preterite is your tense; ongoing or habitual would need imperfect.

english: Where are you from?
tip: English lets 'from' dangle at the end; Spanish forbids it. The preposition leads the question: '¿De dónde eres?' is literally 'From where are you?'

english: Why didn't you come?
tip: "¿Por qué?" (two words, with accent) = Why? "Porque" (one word, no accent) = Because. The accent and spacing matter.

english: I study at the university.
tip: English says 'at' the university; Spanish reaches for en, as if you study inside the institution: estudio en la universidad. Same with en la oficina, en la escuela.

english: The photo came out blurry.
tip: "La foto" – feminine because it's short for "la fotografía." Shortened words keep the gender of the full word.

english: Good morning, how are you?
tip: Why plural? Spanish greetings come in plural: 'Buenos días' = literally 'good days'. Same logic for buenas tardes and buenas noches – always plural.

english: How long have you been here?
tip: "Llevar" + time = to have been (doing something) for (duration). Llevo dos años aquí = I've been here for two years. Very common construction.

english: Do you live with your parents?
tip: Tus is plural because padres is plural – not because of how many 'yous' there are. Spanish possessives agree with the thing owned: tu padre, tus padres, same one owner.

english: What's your dog's name?
tip: Dogs 'call themselves' in Spanish. Names use llamarse: '¿Cómo se llama tu perro?' = literally 'How does your dog call himself?' – cómo, never qué.

english: Don't be late again.
tip: Note 'otra vez': otro/a never takes an indefinite article – it's 'otra vez', never 'una otra vez'.

english: My wife prepares lunch.
tip: 'Mi mujer' = literally 'my woman' – and the everyday word for 'wife' in Spain. Mujer means wife only with a possessive (mi mujer, la mujer de Juan); esposa is the safe-everywhere word.

english: What is your niece's name?
tip: '¿Cómo?' means 'how?' with accent. Without accent, 'como' means 'like/as' or 'I eat.'

english: My hand hurts a lot.
tip: "La mano" is feminine – one of very few -o nouns that are feminine. Memorize it as an exception.

english: The planet needs more trees.
tip: "El planeta" is masculine. Many -a words from Greek/Latin are masculine: planeta, problema, mapa.

english: For how long are you staying?
tip: "Por" for duration: "Estudié por dos horas." Por marks how long something lasted.
